column2: Runs with no display and no human driving a UI — a cron job, a server script, a bot handler. Nobody clicks anything; it runs unattended, server-side.

column1: Two ways to run headless against a remote site — what are they, and what forces the choice?
column2:
headless HTTP client (just `fetch`) vs headless browser (Playwright/Puppeteer, a real Chromium with no window).

The SITE'S AUTH mechanism forces the choice, not the task:
- documented login endpoint returning a token -> fetch
- only a browser session cookie (login is a form POST, no API) -> headless browser (or a human pasting cookies)

column1: When are you FORCED into a headless browser instead of plain fetch?
column2:
Only when the site has no usable API — you must automate typing into the login form, keep the session cookie it sets, and re-script when the HTML shifts.

Costs: a browser binary in your image, brittleness against markup changes, lots of surface to break. Avoid unless auth leaves no choice.

column1: Before automating against an external site, what do you find FIRST, and why?
column2:
The AUTH mechanism — it dictates the whole architecture downstream.

A documented login endpoint returning a token means a plain fetch on a server (cheap, robust, unattended). A browser-session-cookie-only login means a headless browser or manual cookie pasting — barely better than doing it by hand.

Real case: discovering POST /api/auth/manager -> {tokenManager} -> Bearer collapsed the donbass-post upload job from "maybe needs a headless browser" to "a plain fetch".

column1: For an unattended job using a token, how do you handle the token?
column2: Credentials in env, never in the repo. Until you've measured the token's lifetime, fetch a fresh one PER RUN rather than caching — a cached token that silently expires fails the job at the worst time. A 401 mid-run means re-auth, not retry-the-same-token.
